utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. After four weeks of recess, we will now restart. The Chamber was informed that there were a few preliminary matters to be -- oh, no, I first have to -- I've totally gotten out of my routine. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Then I'll resume where I too hastily started with preliminary matters to be raised. Mr. Lukic, the Defence would like raise a matter. You have an opportunity to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you, Your Honour. Good morning. I apologise to interpreters. I will be speaking in two languages. When I quote something from our transcript, I'll read it in English, otherwise I'll be talking in B/C/S. [Interpretation] On 24 July 2014, this Chamber, on page 23648, line 23, and up to page 23653, line 15, issued new instructions to us for the Defence case. I believe that all of these instructions are very restrictive and that they restricts the right of our client to defence. Let us start by saying that our position is that the Rules of the presentation of case cannot be changed mid-case after the Prosecution had its opportunity to present its case. We also believe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I tried to immediately follow your reference, your page reference. For me at this moment, but it may be a technical issue, the transcript of the 24th of July starts at page 24623, whereas you are referring us to page 23648. Is that the slip of the tongue, or is there ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Obviously this has been misrecorded. I said T 24648, line 23.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then I'm with you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We believe that we have the same rights and that we should abide by the same rules that the Prosecutor abided by during the Prosecution case. Otherwise, the rights of our client to fair trial would be seriously threatened. And now I would like to start with the first instruction on page T 24649, line 8. [In English] And I will quote: "To this end, the Chamber notes with concern that many court hours have been spent adducing evidence of questionable relevance, much of which appears at this moment to also have questionable probative value. Many Defence witnesses have given a great deal of evidence about matters that neither appear or form part of any recognisable defence nor relate in any material way to the crimes alleged in the indictment." [Interpretation] With all due respect, we have to point out that we do not agree with this opinion of the Chamber. First of all, we would like to say that a testimony has to be put in a context and has to provide a broader picture of the developments in order to be able to assess the credibility of a witness and to give weight to his or her testimony. Some of the statements prove legitimate defence, although this is not expressly stated. We did not put legal terms into our witnesses' mouths.' We did not write our statements in that way. We used the language that was used by the witnesses themselves. Before the trial started, we asked for the indictment to focus on certain things, and we wanted to be told who exactly were members of the joint criminal enterprise. This never happened. Today we have an indictment in which in Articles 11, 12, and 13, it is stated who members of the joint criminal enterprise are. Apart from the specific names in paragraph 10 of the indictment, in paragraph 11 it is stated that those were members of the leadership of Bosnian Serbs, members of the Serbian Democratic Party, members of the state organs of Bosnian Serbs at the republican regional municipality and local levels including Crisis Staff staffs, War Presidencies, war commissions, commanders, assistant commanders, higher-ranking officers, chiefs of units of the Ministry of the Defence of Serbia, the JNA, the Army of Yugoslavia, the VRS, the Ministry of the Interior of Bosnian Serbs, the Territorial Defence of Bosnian Serbs, at the republican, regional, municipality, and local levels, as well as the leaders of Serbian paramilitary and voluntary units. Article 12 goes even further than that, and it says that all the local Serbs - i.e., all Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina - were members of this joint criminal enterprise. During the pre-trial conferences, this was clarified and it was specified that those were all the Serbs over the age of 16. In the case of an indictment like this, it is absolutely impossible for us, even if we wanted to, to bring and present a wrong witness. Whomever we ask whether they participated in this joint criminal enterprise, we challenge this indictment. Whomever we bring here to testify only about this fact, they are legitimate witnesses who can be presented to this Trial Chamber. Therefore, in the case of such an indictment, it is virtually impossible to locate anybody who was over the age of 16 who resided in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time who is not a suitable witness for this trial. Pursuant to Rule 98 bis, the Defence asked for the scope of the indictment to be reduced. Since nothing has been deleted from this indictment, we have to challenge every single thing. We have to know that in this case after the Prosecution case ended barring bar tabled exhibits, over 3.000 pieces of evidence were tabled and this contributed to the burden on the Defence to challenge the counts of the indictment. As the Trial Chamber already knows, our Defence is also revenge. For example, that people did something in retaliation without that being planned, ordered, or indeed envisaged by Ratko Mladic. Our Defence is also a legitimate response to attacks coming from the other side. We heard the Prosecutor's theory in our case, that the shelling of Sarajevo was aimed at terrorising the civilian population there. According to that -- according to them, this was done without any reason, which is why our witnesses have to explain that the BiH Army nonstop shelled, nonstop opened fire, and the VRS had to respond to those attacks. Whoever testifies about that challenges the indictment. In such cases this could not be a tu quoque defence. This is just challenging the indictment. The Trial Chamber allowed the Prosecutor to go beyond the scope and the geographical range of this indictment. We have the right to defend our client against everything that was presented against him. The Defence should not be held against trying to contest what the Prosecutor did during the Prosecution case relative to the scope of the indictment which was extended. On page T 24649, lines 14 to 16, this is what is objected against us: [In English] "Additionally, during cross-examination, it has often come to the light that the source of a witness's knowledge about a particular incident merely stems from media reports or from the Karadzic defence." [Interpretation] With all due respect, we do not agree with this conclusion reached by the Trial Chamber. The Trial Chamber generalises, erroneously in this case, and the Trial Chamber misunderstands the testimonies of the witnesses who stated that they had been faced with the facts about which they were supposed to testify. In other words, the Karadzic defence was not the source of knowledge for our witnesses. It was the source of questions for them, and I'm talking here primarily about the adjudicated facts. The witnesses do not have any other means of knowing what was accepted as adjudicated facts in any of the other cases if they're not told so. In other words, the Karadzic defence told them what was admitted as adjudicated facts in that case, and they put questions to them about those facts. For example, Witnesses Radojcic and Sehovic, they said that they had seen a picture of Hrasnica which confirmed what they said. It was not Karadzic's defence that informed them about the events -- actually, they showed them something. They showed them a photo which confirmed what they had already known, what they had witnessed during a war. Next, on page 24649, lines 6 through 21, and I quote: [In English] "The Chamber also notes that often these witnesses make sweeping generalisations in their statements which then trigger the Prosecution to spend a great amount of time in cross-examination attempting to show what is readily apparent from the start; that is, that sweeping generalisations have little, if any, probative value." [Interpretation] We believe that as a matter of fact is a generalised statement on the part of the Trial Chamber. We brought and presented very specific, very relevant witnesses for the counts of it -- in the indictment relevant to Sarajevo, because this is the part of the indictment that we have been dealing with so far. We can give you each of the witnesses' names and counts of the indictment that they testified about. We brought battalion commanders, brigade commanders, company commanders who spoke about very specific incidents, and it is not true that their statements are just sweeping generalisations and that they don't have any probative value. It is with regret that we have to say that this type of reasoning on behalf of the Trial Chamber shows that our witnesses are viewed differently than the Prosecution witnesses. The Prosecutor brought several witnesses who did provide sweeping generalisations. For example, their witnesses said, "Serbs destroyed a cultural edifice," and they did not say anything specific about either a possible perpetrator or the way the crime had been done. At the same time, the Trial Chamber and the Prosecutor conducted investigations by examining our witnesses, and that was directed against the members of the Defence team. A lot of time was lost unnecessarily in that. If the Trial Chamber decided to conduct investigations, they should have informed us about the results of those investigations. We believe that we have the right to know. You checked the private e-mails of our witnesses. We ask you to say publicly what you found out; i.e., please inform both us and the general public as well. At the same time, the Defence requested from this Trial Chamber during the testimony of Momir Nikolic to investigate how come that in the report of Bursik, who is the Prosecutor's investigator, that he in his report claimed that Momir Nikolic said something in a recorded conversation which is not true. We want you to inform us whether anything was done, whether there was any investigation about that. If so, what were the results of that investigation? In order to make things even more drastic, the Trial Chamber attacked a member of our team as if we had done something wrong. Now we raise a question: Why the Prosecution Witness Momir Nikolic, who was found by this Tribunal that he was lying, why he wasn't asked how come that he hadn't remembered that before? The first time he ever said that was during the Popovic trial. After that report presented by Bursik, the report which was erroneous, and this was a thing that had to be investigated, we do not have the power like the Prosecutor has to offer relocation, various bargain deals. We believe that when investigation is done, this investigation is channeled in a totally wrong direction. Furthermore, on page 24649, lines 22 through 25, I quote: [In English] "Conversely, relevant content has sometimes been removed from witness statements, apparently triggering the Prosecution's need to explore these subjects as well as the reasons for removing them, all of which needlessly uses a great deal of valuable court time." [Interpretation] I have to tell you, and I have to be very sincere in saying that the Defence was dumbfounded by this finding on the part of the Trial Chamber. The same procedure was used by the Prosecutor when they introduced old statements and compiled new statements of the witnesses in this case or when the Prosecutor used transcripts from the same witnesses' previous testimonies. The Trial Chamber never asked the Prosecutor why they were doing that. Obviously, in such situation, the Defence had to use its valuable time for cross-examination, and this is precisely what the Prosecution has to do now. We don't see anything in dispute here. Why didn't the Trial Chamber ever mention that during the Prosecution case? In that way the Defence would be well informed and in due time that that was a wrong way to do things. Presenting this as a problem at this moment is precisely what constitutes changing the rules of a case at the detriment of the Defence, mid-case. Let's give you a specific example: Witness RM314, the Prosecutor took three statements from him. It has to be known that the statements taken by the Prosecutor are over ten years old, and again there are changes. This has happened all the time. For every Prosecutor witness we received proofing notes about changes, perhaps not for each and every one, but I can easily say that there were over 75 per cent of them. We can present those proofing notes to you if you wish. Witness RM314, the Prosecutor filed his first, second, and third statements. The Prosecutor did not file his proofing notes and his testimony in the Popovic case, which explicitly denies some parts of his previous statements. In other words, the proofing notes and their testimony in the Popovic case change and negate the statements of the same witness that were filed by the Prosecution and admitted by the Trial Chamber. The Prosecution just ignored those things. My colleague Ivetic fought very hard against such an approach by the Prosecution and later by the decision of the Trial Chamber, and you will find that on T 10853. This is just one of the many examples showing how things were changed. Obviously, the Defence had to use a lot of time to correct things that were obvious from the very start. Let me share some more examples with you. RM013, two statements were filed and one set of proofing notes. Witness Ibro Osmanovic, there are three statements, two were admitted as exhibits. Ado Medic, two statements, plus proofing statements presented in the courtroom. Both statements were admitted. RM280, four statements. And the last two are the corrections of the first two statements. All the four statements were admitted into evidence. The Prosecution had 17 years at their disposal to investigate whatever they liked before the trial began. We heard from the Prosecution investigators that they launched investigations as early as 1995; specifically, Investigator Ruez told us so. The Defence had five months to complete its investigation after the last Prosecution witness was heard. I wanted to inform you that we asked for more resources, more personnel, who would be members of our team, and more time. It was not approved. All Defence team members worked tirelessly, nonstop, and to sanction them for not having been allotted the time, the resources, and staff they requested, is not only unjust but also cynical. Let me remind you: In this courtroom on the Prosecution side we saw 26 attorneys who led witnesses. At the beginning, on the Defence side, you saw four attorneys. However, due to the lack of funding, after several of the fist witnesses we had to bring down to only three, and the three who are in the courtroom are not all paid equally as attorneys-at-law, as counsel. We have two paid counsel and one assistant. The next point. At transcript page 24650, line 1, I quote: [In English] "Moreover, the Chamber notes the unfortunate tendency of both parties to adduce evidence that is unnecessarily repetitious or that relates to matters that are not in dispute in the first place; for example, the Chamber has now heard several witnesses give evidence concerning the strength and positions of ABiH units, but when these matters are explored by the Chamber in court it discovers that the parties are more or less in agreement about such facts and there was never a reason to spend court time adducing the evidence to begin with." [Interpretation] I say yet again, it all comes as a consequence of the Prosecution case, the numerous exhibits, and the scope of the indictment. We are prepared to accept any kind of Prosecution stipulation in this matter, and of course any potential Chamber decision as to the location of ABiH army positions, their facilities, warehouses, and command posts in Sarajevo. Of course, unless all positions known to the Defence are accepted where there were ABiH members in Sarajevo, we will keep on leading evidence in that regard. By supporting or corroborative evidence have a particular role to play since they add to the probative value of previous witnesses and the exhibits themselves. The role of such evidence is to deny the evidence led by Prosecution. The next item I have is page 24650, lines 16 to 22. I quote: [In English] "More significantly, the Chamber notes, with serious concern, that witnesses have testified about alarming statement taking practices such as being pressured to sign statements which they knew to contain errors or signing statements that they have not read. A great deal of court time has been used trying to clarify and correct such issues as, for example, those encountered with the statements of Witnesses Deronjic, Batinic, and Tusevljak." [Interpretation] The Defence agrees with this finding as well. We wish to state that the witnesses were not forced to say something. What they said was that they did not have the time to correct their statements but were told that they could do so during their testimony live, which was done every single time. It comes about as a consequence of lack of time, and all such cases happened at the time when we were told that we had to have signed statements. Such mistakes were made only in the course of the following few days following the request by the Chamber. We had to come up with signatures without any delay whatsoever, and it did not provide sufficient time to the Defence to deal with corrections at that point in time, but we did deal with such corrections in our proofing notes and during the main hearing. Nothing was hidden. I will leave the witnesses explained why they had to sign, in what way, and that they were told that they would be accorded an opportunity to have it corrected before the Court and that they were indeed given that opportunity. Page 24651, lines 2 through 4. It was the next objection voiced by the Chamber and the first instruction. I quote: [In English] "First, the parties I expected to limit the production of evidence to matters that are relevant and start by adducing evidence which is most important" -- or "relevant," actually, sorry. [Interpretation] This is new and it was not in place during the Prosecution case, although it is stated that it refers to both sides but the Prosecution was no longer leading its evidence. It is therefore clear that this instruction only affects the Defence. We believe that the Defence has a right to decide on its own order or presentation. We believe that at this stage the Chamber has no right to influence our decision on presentation order. At this point in time, it is unclear why the Defence is leading that particular evidence before some other. Such assessment could only be done at the close of our case. The next point is on page 24651, lines 4 through 7. I quote: [In English] "The Chamber reminds the parties that relevant evidence has been defined by the Appeals Chamber as evidence relating to a material issue and that the material issue of a case are to be found in the indictment." [Interpretation] Precisely. We saw what the indictment is. We simply cannot miss by responding to it. We have no problem with this particular standard to be applied. We believe that all our evidence is relevant, and we believe that our evidence needs to be viewed in a more -- in a wider context at all times. Of course this is not something the Prosecution finds to its liking, but we don't know why the Chamber shares that view. Our evidence cannot be understood unless viewed in totality. This Defence is not afraid of the truth. Everything is being pronounced tu quoque. Anything that aims at providing a wider context, it is impossible to avoid this wider context in the situation in which all Serbs older than 16 in 1992 were members of the same JCE. We wish to show you that there were several levels, and that is why we bring witnesses who may not have participated in a specific operation but, for example, the man in question was the municipal head at the time and under the indictment he was a JCE member. He is a relevant witness who needs to say whether the JCE existed and what was it that the members of that JCE did. Of course we don't only lead soldiers as witnesses who had participated in particular operations. The next point. Page 24651, line 7 to line 9. I quote: [In English] "Inasmuch as the Defence finds it preferable to use witness statements from other trials, it is expected to remove irrelevant material from such statements before they are tendered in this case." [Interpretation] In addition to this general or generalised indictment, the Defence was put in a position to listen to Prosecution evidence which did not refer to directly. When one of the last few or perhaps the very last Prosecution witness was examined, we also found out that the indictment included something that is not in the text itself which is the time before the relevant period in 1995 as well as a specific geographic location in Croatia. You can find it in the witness testimony provided by Theunens at transcript page 20318 and onwards. We now have to deal with Croatia it seems. And we also have to deal with the period of time before the 12th of May, 1992. Who is to blame for that? Not the Defence and it cannot be held responsible. The next point, page 24651, lines 13 through 16. I quote: [In English] "In short, this means that the Defence should avoid adducing evidence including in written statements for which there is no factual basis or which could be characterised as a sweeping generalisation." [Interpretation] We believe, in this case as well, that this part of the Chamber's instructions should also reflect the situation in this case; i.e., the indictment needs to be taken into account as well as the statement by the Prosecution that they would go beyond the scope of that time in both temporal and geographical terms. Of course, one also needs to bear in mind the enormous amount of documents filed by the Prosecution that we need to respond to. I'm nearing the end, and I would kindly ask for a little bit of patience. On page 24651, lines 24 through to line 6 on the next page, the Chamber states the following in item 4, I quote: [In English] I'm sorry if I said item 4, it's item 3, third. "Third, the Chamber expects the parties to carefully consider the necessity of adducing repetitious or background evidence. The Chamber reminds the Defence that should it wish to offer evidence that is, for example, cumulative in nature or which relates to the historical, political, or military background of the case, it should seek to do so pursuant to Rule 92 bis, a Rule created precisely for the purpose of expanding complex trials by eliminating the need to use court time for adducing such evidence."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I take it was a slip of the tongue when you wanted to say "expediting" rather than "expanding."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Expediting, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. [Interpretation] In what kind of situation are we at this moment? Before proposing the signed witness statements, we did our own research and we often realised that statements contain elements of background facts as well as the context as well as addressing the acts and conduct of General Mladic. They oftentimes also included things that should not be in those statements under 92 bis but should enter under 92 ter. Given the fact that the Rules do not allow for a statement to be filed that contains something that has a direct bearing on the accused needs to be introduced through 92 bis. The fact that such statements contain background information and historical context is no reason for rejecting them, especially if it is known that the Defence is -- does not waste time on it because it had already been contained in the statement, and the Prosecution needs to assess whether there is any need to go into questioning such background and historical facts. Or, rather, to simply focus on the gist of the statement, which is the acts and conduct of General Mladic. I thank you for having given me this opportunity to state our position regards the remarks the few days before the recess and we could not respond to it at that point in time. That is why I thank you again for this opportunity. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Could I seek some clarification. Page 16, line 13, start with the word "needs..." I reread your sentence. You said: "Given the fact that the Rules do not allow for a statement to be filed that contains something that has a direct bearing on the accused needs to be introduced through 92 bis ..." May I understand you wanting to say that does not allow for a statement to be filed that contains something that has a direct bearing under the accused to be introduced through 92 bis?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Exactly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and you were, as I understand from what you later said, you were not talking about a direct bearing but about acts and conduct. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think that it's acts and conduct and bearings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Because we have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- not what the Rules says, but let's have --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Usually they combine all three, and usually you can find it at the end of the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. I leave it to that at the moment. I tend to agree that at least if it's about acts and conduct of the accused that it may have a direct bearing, whether the -- it's true the other way around is, I think, still to be something to be thought of. Again, thank you, Mr. Lukic. Does the Prosecution wish to respond, and if so, now or at a later stage?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I could speak for probably three minutes and address at least an initial response to the Defence comments. I think for the purposes of today --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, as a matter of fact, I'd like you to either to -- not to start now but a little bit and then later expound to it. So could you please make up your mind as to whether you want to respond now or at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, we disagree rather strongly with many of the comments made by the Defence. We are willing, if the Trial Chamber would like, to submit separate individualised responses to some of the allegations made during the statement. Otherwise, it's well-established law that matters of practice, procedure, and the general conduct of the proceedings are well within the Trial Chamber's discretion. So with that, Your Honour, I think those are our comments for now. If the Chamber would like to have -- like us to address some of the specific examples that were raised by the Defence, we're certainly willing to submit submissions with respect to those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there are any specifics where you think it would be appropriate to deal with them, then the Chamber would preferably receive any comments in writing. Then we are five minutes away from the break. There were other preliminary matters, I do understand, from the Prosecution. And perhaps if I understood the gist of at least one of the preliminary matters to be raised by the Prosecution, well, I wonder whether the following might even remove the necessity to deal with it because the Chamber would like to briefly deal with the revised translation of P6690. The Chamber admitted P6690 into evidence on the 23rd of July, 2014, during the testimony of Milan Pejic. On the 19th of August the Prosecution advised the Chamber and the Defence through an informal communication that it had requested and received a revised English translation of this exhibit. That has now been uploaded in e-court under doc ID 1D08-10188-A. I did misspeak and I'll repeat because the transcriber indeed copied exactly my mistake. I'll repeat: Uploaded into e-court under doc I ID 1D08-0188-A. Upon agreement of the Defence, which I received on the 24th of August, 2014, through an informal communication, the Chamber hereby instructs the Registry to replace the current translation with the revised version. But there was another matter, I do understand, Ms. Bibles, that you wanted to raise. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Your Honour, the Defence did provide additional witness statements to the Prosecutor on the 15th of August. We now have statements for 152 prospective witnesses. I would simply put, for the purposes of the record, that according to the agreement between the parties, for those witnesses for whom we do not have statements they are either experts or internationals, witnesses for whom Karadzic or Popovic statements may be used, or the witnesses will be called viva voce. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for raising that issue. I put it on the record. As far as experts are concerned, the Chamber will deal with them rather soon. But there is one item which may even need urgent attention, and I'll deal with that in the remaining two minutes. On the -- it's about the safe conduct motion. On the 12th of August of this year, the Defence filed a safe conduct motion for a witness who is scheduled to testify during the first week of September. As the Registrar requires some time to process safe conduct orders, the Chamber would like to ask the Defence to consider rescheduling the appearance of that witness in order to allow: First of all, the Chamber sufficient time to consider the motion; and second, the Registry sufficient time to process the order should the Chamber decide to grant the motion. Then finally, since we've got one minute left, I will deal with P6649, which is a criminal report dated the 26th of October, 1992. On the 9th of July of this year, P6649 was tendered and marked for identification as a confidential document. On the 24th of July, the Chamber admitted P6649 into evidence, and the Chamber hereby clarifies that P6649 is admitted into evidence under seal. I leave it to that for the time being, although there are a few matters the Chamber would like to raise pretty soon. We first take a break and we'll resume at 10 minutes to 11.00 and expect the Defence then to be ready to call its next witness. We take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have a bit of a late start. That's due to some urgent matters we had to deal with. Apologies for that. Is the Defence ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We are, Your Honour. The next witness is Goran Sehovac, testifying without any protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could Mr. Sehovac be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may, before the witness is brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I spoke with Mr. Traldi and we agreed that the Defence will use with our Witness GRM251 statement -- his statement marked as 1D1773 instead of 1D169. When the witness is here, we filed both statements. You will see that there are some cosmetic changes and you can explore with the witness how it comes that he signed both statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And that's the third witness to appear this week.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning Mr. Sehovac.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration, the text of which is now handed out to you. You do not hear -- can you hear the interpreters now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Sehovac, before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration, the text of which is now handed out to you, and I'd like to invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sehovac. Please be seated. Mr. Sehovac, you'll first be examined by Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Ivetic is a member of the Defence team of Mr. Mladic. Mr. Ivetic, if you're ready, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: Good morning to you, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to call up in e-court 1D01609, and I have a hard copy -- a clean hard copy for the witness. With the usher's assistance and the co-operation of the Prosecution counsel, we could perhaps already get that to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, on the screen in front of you I would direct your attention to the signature. On the first page of the Serbian, can you identify that signature?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Whose signature is it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: This is my own signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now I'd like to turn to the last page of the document in the Serbian original.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, could you confirm for us whose signature is located on this page?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: We are talking about the last page; right? Yes, this is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Subsequent to signing this statement for the Defence team of General Mladic, did you have occasion to review the same in proofing with myself in the Serbian language?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I did make some minor changes, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to take a look together at paragraph 9 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Page 3 in the Serbian, page 2 in the English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In the last line of that paragraph you say that you have personal knowledge of civilians being used as human shields. Can you explain that phrase for us?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: No, not personal knowledge. This was misrecorded. However, at that moment I was in that area in Nedzarici on the front line facing the city of Sarajevo. In that part of Nedzarici the Serbs were fleeing using their own secret roads across the line, and those people talked to us when they crossed over to our territory. They told us what was going on in the city of Sarajevo and how the police treated those civilians, how the civilians were being pushed among the soldiers in order to create an erroneous picture of what was going on. This means that I heard that from the people who had left Sarajevo, who had fled Sarajevo. Those are the Serbs who found themselves in Sarajevo when the war started, and they used covert roads to cross the lines and join us in Nedzarici. That's the explanation of that part of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now if we can look at paragraph 10 which is the same page in the Serbian and is on page 3 in the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we do so, Witness, are you in a position to tell us any name of any of those persons that told you this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I? Well, listen, it was a long time ago, over 20 plus years. Those people left --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you don't have to explain why there was a good reason not to know. Do you have a name? If so, please give it; if you don't have names, please tell us as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can look now at paragraph 10, which is on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Here you talk about the situation in Vares and you say that you establish a line at Brgule, facing part of Croatia. Do you have a clarification here?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: That was not Croatian territory. We established our line in Brgule. That part was controlled by the BH army together with the HVO. So that was that. That was not Croatia. That was a territory partly controlled by the HVO. That's where we established our line. The Croatian civilians and troops were a majority there, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we can turn to paragraph 14 of your statement, which is on page 3 in the English, and crosses between pages 3 and 4 in the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Here you talk about a Franciscan monastery and the priests, friars, and students leaving. Were you present at the time that they left?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: No, no. I was not there. According to what I know, they left of their own will. However, throughout the war the Franciscan monastery in question was guarded and protected.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now apart from these clarifications to your written statement, do you stand behind the same as being accurate?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: Of course, fully. I'm here to defend the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I were to ask you the same questions about the same topics today, would your answers in substance be the same?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And having taken the solemn declaration to tell the truth today, would those answers, as contained in your written statement, be truthful?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: As a citizen of Bosnia-Herzegovina, i.e. Republika Srpska, I am duty-bound to tell the truth. This is why I'm here.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I at this time tender the written statement 1D01609 as a public exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In the absence of any objection, Madam Registrar, the number would be...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D01609 receives number D596, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have a summary to read of the witness's testimony which has been given to the booths and which has been explained to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The witness was a young soldiers from the Nedzarici settlement in Sarajevo. In mid-1992 he was sent to do his compulsory military service at the VRS in Han Pijesak where after two months of training he was assigned to the anti-terrorist unit of the protection regiment. During this time his unit was sent to protect territories in the areas of Zepa, Zvornik, and Vlasenica. In 1993 the witness was assigned to the military police of the Ilidza Brigade as a resident of that area. In early 1994, the assault detachment of the military police was formed and the witness became its member. He stayed in that position for the duration of the war. The witness knows that civilians were fitted with explosives by the ABiH and forced towards the Serb lines. The witness's father saved several such persons. In 1993 the witness and his unit received orders to assist the threatened Croatian civilians in Vares, at which time these Croats were provided security and given the option of staying on Serb territory or continuing to Croat lines. His unit accomplished this task successfully. The Franciscan monastery at Nedzarici was also under the protection of the VRS, and the only damage came from ABiH fire. The witness states that he was under orders to allow humanitarian aid arriving from Butmir airport to cross through check-points unhindered after performing a superficial cursory examination. There was one striking incident where the witness personally found ammunition in a food shipment. This was covered by the media. He knows of other such incidents, including when gunpowder was found in oxygen tanks intended for hospital use. This completes the summary of the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you have any further questions, Mr. Ivetic, you may put them to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sehovac, I do have some follow-up questions. To start with, if we look back at paragraph number 2, page 2 of both versions of your statement, here you talk about being a soldier who had not done compulsory military service. Can you please explain to us how it is that you came to know that the SDA had stolen the military records?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: May I? As a teenager, at the time I was 18, according to the rules of the then Yugoslav and under the law of the then Yugoslav, all lads who come of age have the right to serve in the JNA. It was a lovely custom in the former Yugoslavia. All the nations and nationalities sent their sons to the army irrespective of whether they were Serbs, Croats, or Muslims. We all served in the army together. We learned how to defend our homeland. But the Bosniak policies, i.e. the Bosniak political party, the SDA, which stole documents in Novi Grad. But first I need to explain that every municipality had its recruiting centre where documents were kept regarding all the lads who were to be recruited into the JNA. At Novi Grad municipality is a big municipality, one of the biggest ones in the city of Sarajevo, and there were a lot of administrative workers in the municipality. At that moment my parents, as well as the parents of all the other lads - Muslims, Croats, and Serbs - prepared us for service in the JNA, i.e. in the common army. However, that didn't happen because the SDA stole the documents or moved them away or burned them of all the lads residing in the municipality of Novi Grad. I don't know how that happened. I wouldn't be able to tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could you tell us how you found out? That was the question. And -- but if you say, "I don't know how that happened," where you said before that they stole them or moved them away or burned them, does this mean that you do not know whether they were stolen or burned or moved away?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My father learned that, i.e., the information leaked from the municipality of Novi Grad. At that moment, my father was preparing a party to send me off into the army. However, the information was leaked by the administrative workers of the municipality; those people who worked at the municipality informed my father that the documents had gone missing and that nobody from Novi Grad would be sent to serve in the JNA. That's the line of information. Since everybody knew each other, there were Serbs, Muslims, and Croats there, I suppose that a Serb double-checked that information and learned that the documents had been stolen and informed not only my father but all the other parents whose sons were about to be recruited into the JNA. To put it simply: The objective was to boycott the JNA, to prevent citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina from serving in the JNA. That's the explanation of some people from that political party. At that time as a young lad, I could not understand that somebody could commit such a crime against the sovereignty of its own state, a state that we all lived for. My father was very disappointed with the fact that I was not going to serve in the army, because he was a member of the League of Communists and he was a Yugoslav at heart.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did Your Honour have additional follow-ups?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I leave it to you at this moment, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, if we can now focus on your compulsory military service with the VRS in Han Pijesak. And you say that the training lasted two months at paragraph 3. Can you tell us what kind of training you underwent at that time including the topics of that training?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: All sorts of incidents started occurring all around Bosnia-Herzegovina, and especially in Sarajevo. Our Crisis Staff in Nedzarici, somewhat older people in it, gathered all the young men and advised them to go and serve in the JNA. As a result of that, all of us lads gathered in Han Pijesak, that was our base because the barracks were there and all the recruits arrived there, they were deployed across various units, and they were trained. How were they trained? One part of that training was theory and the other part was practical training. Every army does that: Theory and practice. Theoretical training regarded the conduct of a soldier in service: How should a soldier behave in the case of war; how to treat prisoners of war; military officers; what does a soldier do confronted by many civilians. After that it was handling all sorts of fire-arms. That training was the result of an order received by our command. They were supposed to speed things along because combat had started around Han Pijesak, around Zepa, and the entire territory of Romanija. The expedited training that we completed in Han Pijesak had me sent to the PT unit or the protection regiment. The PT stands for "anti-terrorist unit" which was part of the military police. The mission of that unit was to military policing and defence of the territory where they were deployed. In other words, they were supposed to protect the sovereignty of the Yugoslav Peoples' Army. We thought that it was still the Yugoslav Peoples' Army but that was transformed into the Army of Republika Srpska as the war started.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, you say that while you were a member of the anti-terrorist unit's military police, you were given the toughest tasks in Zepa, Zvornik, and Vlasenica. Can you just briefly give us more detail about what you were doing there and why? Why was it necessary?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: First of all, the military police received very difficult tasks. The war had literally begun by that time and the military police was supposed to keep order among soldiers and the people who had been recruited or were reservists. That is why the military police intervened when there were disturbances of law and order and when people disrespected the law of Republika Srpska and its armed forces. The anti-terrorist unit had that as its principal task as well as to implement all orders of its military command when it comes to its own soldiers. All VRS soldiers had to be brought in if they refused to implement their duties. Another goal of the anti-terrorist unit was the one that had to do with the war. I can address that in detail. When we were sent to the area of Zepa, to Laze, I believe, we came across a police APC, a civilian police APC, that had been hit by an anti-armour asset. I came across two dead policemen there. It was my first stressful situation, so to speak, because it was my first time to see some dead people. I entered the APC to extract the bodies, and I remember well that one of the policemen had sneakers on. They were basically not killed by bullets. They probably tried to look out of the APC and received a bullet to the head, and due to a detonation the other bodies were shattered inside. Our goal was to pull out those people and then we retreated to Laze where there was some kind of facility. I think before the war it had been a school. We were trapped there and we spent some 10 to 15 days in encirclement. That is that regarding Laze. We managed to pull out a fortnight later. Some elderly people, locals, managed to break through the line from Sokolac and reach us. They basically left their homes to bring all of us, the boys, out. We were all between 18 and 20. Out of the 60 that we started off with, only around 20 able-bodied soldiers were left. That is that regarding that particular incident. We also went Crni Vrh. It was a critical point en route to Zvornik. That is the area where our civilians from Sarajevo came, using that route to flee to Serbia with their children. Many ABiH soldiers went through that area as well in their attempt to reach Tuzla, killing our civilians in the process. According to our information, Naser Oric's unit controlled that area on the side of the ABiH. We had prevailed over them on several occasions before at Crni Vrh securing the route for the mothers and children and other civilians to traverse the critical area.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to move on as we are short with time. I'd like to focus on the Croat population in Vares that is discussed at paragraphs 10 through 12 of your statement at page 3 in both versions. And, first of all, you say in your statement that: "The threatened citizens of Vares, predominantly Croats ..." How were they being threatened and by whom?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: You see, it was never clear to me. The war in Bosnia-Herzegovina as a whole remains unclear to me. It is a very ugly thing that happened and I wish no one suffers the same fate ever again. It isn't clear to me that the Croats and Muslims tied their -- would tie their flags together in Sarajevo. As an observer on the VRS side, we established our line at Brgule, towards their territory, because we had been informed that the army of BiH would attack RS territory. And our goal was only to defend, never to attack. We were to defend it at any cost. All of a sudden we could hear artillery fire and we thought the RS was being attacked. I woke up, I didn't understand anything, and I saw in Vares and its environs and villages there, I don't know their names because I do not hail from that territory, it is foreign to me, but I could see that there was a war there. We were told by our Ilidza Brigade command to get ready in case of attack, because the ABiH apparently had attacked the HVO, the territory controlled by the Croats. It was completely unclear to us. We literally simply observed and did not wish to get involved. It was a conflict between the Muslims and Croats, but we were also told that there were many civilians, children, and mothers, as well as the elderly in Vares who were unable to defend themselves. We were asked if we were ready to intervene in order to save them. As a soldier, as a Serb, as a Yugoslav, I was proud to be issued that order. I said that I would save every last person if I can together with the VRS and my unit, and that the command was to discuss it with our neighbouring units to lend a hand as well. There were many units there. Our order was to go halfway to Vares and that the civilians would be fleeing in our direction. In Vares the civilians had been told that they could freely go towards VRS lines, that they would be welcomed there. The first people that I came upon was a mother with two children, one of whom had fallen down. I placed both girls on my back and invited their mother to follow me. We went through the woods and reached Brgule. There was a column of people following, many civilians. It was our task only to simply physically secure them. The Army of BiH, I have to say, constantly targeted that part of the forest. They couldn't see through the forest and were not successful in targeting the civilians, but the Ilidza Brigade and the military police sustained between 10 and 15 wounded soldiers. I was also lightly injured, thank God not seriously.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: I was grazed by a bullet.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I could interrupt you and ask you, sir, if you know how many Croat civilians were assisted in this manner from Vares?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: One moment, one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We don't receive interpretation. Could you please restart your answer, the question being how many Croat civilians were assisted in this manner from Vares?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I go on? First I have to say that it was an interesting task and a challenging one for me and the entire brigade and its military police. It was a difficult one because on the Serb side many parents had lost their children. Their sons were being killed in different areas where Serbs engaged Croats. It was very difficult to secure those civilians because people might react and open fire at them. There were some small groups surfacing here and there, between 5 and 10, mostly criminals, and our order was to sanction them, so to speak, and if they disobeyed they were to be arrested if they disturbed the civilians. We managed to secure the civilians and remove those groups. We placed the civilians in an encirclement, secured them, and we successfully executed the task. I am proud that as a VRS soldier I helped those civilians and I keep meeting them all over Bosnia-Herzegovina to this day. Now how many were there? They were starved and when we ordered food from our quartermaster's service to feed them, I could see that we requested between 3- and 3-and-a-half thousand servings, there were that many people.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like to turn paragraph 16 found at page 3 in both versions of your statement where you talk about a humanitarian convoy that had NATO rifle ammunition, and you talk about a video.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would like to at this moment call up video D472, and I will not be playing the video nor the audio but I have selected a freeze-frame portion from that video at 20 seconds into the exhibit, and it should be visible if we switch over to the Defence monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I would ask you to take a look at this freeze-frame of this video and tell us if you recognise anyone who is depicted in this portion of the video.

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: That is me dressed in a military police uniform. I was checking a UN vehicle. It is me until the camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And is this the incident that is described in paragraph 16 of your written statement?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, that is the very incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can I ask to clarify, I see two people in camouflage uniforms. Can you tell, is it you who is visible in the middle of the picture or on the right side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The person in the middle. I'm much younger and much thinner, please do not be confused. But the person in the middle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fewer kilos.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you have a recollection of the month or time of year that this incident occurred?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: Of course. It was sometime in 1993, perhaps March or April. One of the two. I don't know the exact date. I cannot recall it. In any case, March or April. I remember it well. If need be, I can describe the incident itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We have that in your statement. I'd like to move on since we are pressed for time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I have just have one question --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- on this paragraph. Sir, how did you establish that the rifle ammunition with a caliber of 5.56 millimetre belonged to NATO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see, when we were informed our captain, the late Obrad Popadic, was informed that there was a suspicious load moving towards Butmir -- well, let me clarify first: All aid and all UNPROFOR vehicles moved freely through the territory of the municipality of eastern Ilidza. There was never any problem and there were strict orders in place that no vehicle should be bothered, that they would go through freely save for some routine checks in order to avoid potential criminal activities. We checked the container and found two types of ammunition, one was 5.56 and the other was 12.7 millimetre calibre. It's not in the statement, but I remember well that there were two kinds of ammunition: 5.56 millimetre ammunition is for rifles and 12.7 for machine-guns. I could establish that because I was a soldier and I know very well what kind of weapons uses what kind of bullet and calibre. I hope this suffices.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That doesn't suffice because you haven't answered my question. My question is: How did you determine that this ammunition belonged to NATO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, who was driving the truck? Was it me? It was an international community vehicle. You would have to ask them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, sir. You have written in your statement that it belonged to NATO. How did you establish that this ammunition belonged to NATO? If you don't know how you established, you are just guessing, you can say so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was an UNPROFOR vehicle transporting the cargo. Anything onboard an UNPROFOR truck is UNPROFOR property. That is how we drew the conclusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And it is up to the court to prove it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I'm simply trying to explain that it was an international community vehicle owned by UNPROFOR. All cargo on such vehicles -- I do have some kind of education. If there is such cargo on a vehicle, it is a criminal act unless it is on the bill of lading and approved. The ammunition was not and it was being taken to Butmir and Hrasnica. It was an international community UNPROFOR vehicle. I am not in the position or do not have the competence to examine who that ammunition belonged to. It was in the vehicle and as a soldier I'm saying that it was found in an UNPROFOR vehicle. I do not wish to be misunderstood, and I wish to address you with the utmost respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You obviously didn't know who it belonged to. All you know is that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Don't talk when I'm talking. From your answer I take it that you don't know who the ammunition belonged to. All you know is that it was in an UNPROFOR vehicle. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have one short follow-up question: Is UNPROFOR the same as NATO for you? Yes, I see that you are nodding "yes." Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, in the arsenals of the JNA --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry, the translation has not yet come in of your question, I'm told.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I saw the witness nodding "yes." I asked you whether UNPROFOR was the same as NATO for you and I saw you nodding in the affirmative; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no. You misunderstood me. At that time there was only UNPROFOR and we co-operated with them. There is no dispute about that. I do not connect NATO and UNPROFOR. I don't think that they are one and the same thing. They are two different things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second then, please. Mr. Mladic, if you once again --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you once again --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you once again communicate with the witness in the way you did it before, laughing, et cetera, you know what the result will be. You'll be removed from the courtroom. Then I -- one second, please, again. And the same, Witness, is for you: You don't have to salute to the accused in this courtroom. You should not in any way communicate with him, even without words. Mr. Mladic, no demonstrations. Sit down. You know --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No speaking aloud, Mr. Mladic. Once again, you'll be removed from the courtroom if it once ... The Chamber doesn't like the little games you are playing. One second please, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Perhaps if I can ask the Prosecution is there any dispute that 5.56 calibre ammunition is NATO-grade ammunition?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My question was to test the -- not the ammunition but the knowledge of the witness about NATO and UNPROFOR. In your statement, Witness, you say it was NATO rifle ammunition, and your explanation in court you said you concluded that it was NATO because it was in UNPROFOR hands, which seems to -- that you are mixing up the two. Because UNPROFOR -- if it's not NATO, how could you possibly conclude from it being transported by UNPROFOR that it was NATO ammunition? Any explanation for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I? Yes, yes. As a soldier at the time, I was not specialised in either NATO or UNPROFOR. We were told it was NATO ammunition and the vehicle belonged to UNPROFOR. NATO did not exist at that time, but we were told it was NATO ammunition; i.e., people from the command told us that it was NATO ammunition and the vehicle - or, rather, the vehicles - that transported that ammunition were UNPROFOR vehicles. That's the explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic. By the way, you had used already 33 minutes before the question --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- put by Judge Moloto. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I will be brief. I only have about three questions left.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What was the calibre of rifle ammunition used by the JNA and by the VRS?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: 7.62. The VRS never used the other kind of calibre. We did not have the weapons for this type of ammunition, which is why I can tell you that we had automatic rifles that used calibre 7.62. It's a well-known and widely used calibre, so I'm -- I suppose you know what I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I do. Now, as a member of the Ilidza Brigade's military police, did you ever receive orders to terrorise the civilian population of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: No. That was not our priority. Moreover, as military policemen, we toured the lines and we would tell all the people never to use weapons against the civilians. Unless there was a BiH Army attack against Ilidza, if the line was at risk, then they were instructed to destroy the enemy, but not civilians only the troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you ever hear of VRS snipers be ordered to be engaged against Sarajevo civilian targets?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: No, there were no such cases at all. Just the opposite was the case. The BiH Army constantly opened fire on Nedzarici and Ilidza. They opened sniper fire on the two. I never received such an order. Nobody was ever ordered to terrorise civilians. That was not our objective. Our sole objective was to defend the territory of the Serbian municipality of Ilidza, which is what we did at the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I thank you for your answers to my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no more direct. But, again, I would ask the Prosecution if there is an agreement as to NATO-grade ammunition being 5.56 millimetres and Warsaw Pact being 7.62 millimetres and that is a notorious fact in how these ammunitions are called in the military industry.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I don't believe that was the issue that was at the heart of the matter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: -- with the witness, so I'm happy to check into that, and then if there's -- yes, I believe there is an expert on this point that testified to some of the matters. So if I could just check something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: It might be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- after the break --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: -- in the evidence anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So after the break -- well, yes, if something is in evidence it doesn't mean that it's not challenged.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not the same. But if you presented evidence to that extent, then we'd like to hear from you and that there is no dispute about it. Please proceed. Witness, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Weber. You'll find him to your right. Mr. Weber is counsel for the Prosecution. And may I ask you to focus very much on answering the question that is put to you and not to dwell away from what was asked. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: Good morning to you, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Today on page 29 you were recorded as stating: "Our Crisis Staff in Nedzarici, somewhat older people in it, gathered all the young men and advised them to go and serve in the JNA." When did this happen?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: That happened - just a moment - in mid-June 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Who was it that advised you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: What do you mean when you ask me who advised me? Do you want me to give you the name of a person?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes, I'm asking you who are the individuals, their names, that advised you.

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: All our parents, my father, for example, who -- and then Mr. Radivoje Grgovic, who was subsequently elected as the commander of the Nedzarici Battalion. All of our parents. They had sat down together knowing that we would not be serving in the JNA because the political party, the SDA, had stolen our documents. As a result of that, our parents decided to send us to Han Pijesak to serve in the army there instead of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, sir --

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: Which means that we volunteered to serve.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, if you could please focus on my questions, the particular information that I'm asking. Was Mr. Grgovic a member of the Crisis Staff in Nedzarici?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In paragraph 3 of your statement, you indicate that you were assigned to a part of General Mladic's protection regiment in 1992. Was this regiment the 65th Motorised Protection Regiment?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: It was the protection regiment in Crna Rijeka. We were the first generation of young lands, young soldiers, who became members of that protection regiment. Its name was the protection regiment of the Army of Republika Srpska. Our base was in Han Pijesak or, rather, Crna Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: This was the 65th Motorised Protection Regiment; correct? Sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, was it the 65th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, I was a soldier there and that was not its name. It was the first protection regiment of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'll go at it a different way. In the same paragraph you indicate that Velibor Sotra was your company commander. Can you please tell us the name of his commander, his immediate superior?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: Velibor Sotra was an officer in the anti-terrorist unit, and Milomir Savic was the commander of the protection regiment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. And, thank you, that is helpful. This regiment was directly subordinated to the VRS Main Staff; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us precisely what months you went through training once you joined the VRS?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: July and August 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us when it was that you were in the field in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: I was not in Zvornik. I was in Crni Vrh, which is in the Zvornik region. I just explained that a while ago. We secured the transversal road used by the civilians to go to Zvornik. This area belongs to the Zvornik region.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, if you could please focus on my questions. I'm just asking you when it was that you were in the Zvornik area, and you've explained that you were in Crni Vrh.

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: The period when I was in Crni Vrh was sometime in September.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: What about Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: In order to get there we had to go through Vlasenica all the time. We were not engaged there. We were involved in military policing, which means we instilled order among the troops of the Army of Republika Srpska. If somebody committed a breach of discipline, we would intervene. We were not engaged in any war operations. We just did our regular military policing jobs in that part of the municipality of Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could you then lastly, please, tell us when was the period of time in which you were in the field in Zepa, in the Zepa area?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: October. Late September, early October.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: That would be of the year 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could you please give us the dates in which you were a member of the protection regiment? From when until when?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: From the end of June or early July until the end of the year 1992, and that also included the training period.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. During this time, aside from the training that you had in the -- in the early part and the areas that you've mentioned, were you stationed in Crna Rijeka?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I see it is possibly time for a break. I'm about to start into something new.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we take the break now. Could the witness first be escorted out of the courtroom. We will take a break of 20 minutes. And we will resume at 20 minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue with the witness, the Chamber would like to briefly deal with the Defence's request to vary the trial sitting schedule. On the 13th of June of this year, the Defence requested the Chamber to permanently move from the current five-day schedule to a four-day sitting schedule with Wednesdays being designated non-sitting days. And this can be found at transcript page 22670. After the filing of the latest medical expert reports, the Prosecution, on the 5th of August of this year, agreed to a four-day sitting schedule. The Defence renewed its request in writing on the 7th of August, 2014, additionally seeking a four-hour day schedule as well as automatic days of rest in the event the accused suffers an emotional crisis or a transient ischemic attack. The Chamber -- and perhaps, Mr. Usher, you could already get the witness on standby. The Chamber hereby grants the Defence's request in part and orders that a four-day sitting schedule shall be adopted, provisionally Friday being designated as the non-sitting day, apart from Monday the 15th of September, which shall be the non-sitting day in the week starting on that day. All other requests are dismissed, including the request to shorten the daily sitting hours. The Chamber will provide reasons for this decision in writing in due course. The Chamber will address the preference of the Defence to not sit on Wednesday and will inquire with medical experts about the medical basis for a specific non-sitting day. The Chamber, Mr. Lukic, assumed that where the sitting schedule was still a five-day schedule that we could start this week, perhaps to leave out the last witness, and already start a four-day week already this week, that means not sitting on this Friday. Or would that cause you any problems?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It would not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And perhaps it even could be if that witness has not arrived which is scheduled for later this week that his arrival could be delayed so as to avoid --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll see into it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- unnecessary -- okay. May I take it, Mr. Weber, that it doesn't cause any problem for the Prosecution either?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, before proceeding, if I could report back to the Chamber on the 5.56 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: -- millimetre ammunition. The Prosecution is unable to agree to the proposed fact due to evidence in the record about this type of ammunition and the VRS. A quick search revealed some examples, and I just provide them quickly on the record. P4404, page 5 in the B/C/S and page 8 in the English; and P355, one of General Mladic's notebooks, specifically an entry from 23 September, 1992, which is located at page 115 in the English. So thank you for the opportunity for us to look into that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And do you mean to say that reference is made there to 5.56 millimetre ammunition in the -- not in NATO but, rather, in other hands?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I take it that you'll have a look at it --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: But, Your Honours, that does not address my request for stipulation, which I repeat from page 42, line 3 through 7. I asked the Prosecution if there is an agreement as to NATO-grade ammunition being 5.56 millimetres and Warsaw Pact being 7.62 millimetres and that this is a notorious fact as to how these ammunitions are called in the military industry. I had nothing to do with the VRS. 5.562 in its name is NATO ammunition, Your Honours. That's what I'm getting at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. I do not know what the difference is between the name and the calibre itself, so you would call it different from what the real calibre is. Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In the military industry, 5.52 by 43 millimetres is called NATO cartridges.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: 56, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
