utterances.text: Okay. Well, that's -- well, apparently there is no agreement on that. I take it that the issue was whether by the mere calibre of the ammunition found, whether that would be an indication as to where it may have come from.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Exactly, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That, apparently, is not resolved by the -- by a stipulation. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Sehovac, in paragraph of your statement, you state: "In 1993 at the request of Obrad Popadic, who is in command of a unit in Ilidza at the time, I was assigned to that unit as a resident of Sarajevo." Obrad Popadic was the deputy commander of the Ilidza Brigade up until May 1994; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: When did you make this request in 1993? Or when was this request in 1993?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: Captain Obrad Popadic made that request in 1992 and sent it to the command of the protection regiment. He addressed it to me. He stated that he needed me in Ilidza, he needed military policemen, and since I was well familiar with the area he thought that I would be of great use to him there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, please focus on my question. I was just asking you when. Are you able to provide us anymore specificity aside from in 1992 this request was made?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: He made the request in 1992. And then in late 1992 on the eve of the new year I was assigned to the Ilidza Brigade. I joined from the protection regiment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. That -- that helps out answer one thing. But just going back to the request, was that made well before you joined the protection regiment or right beforehand -- or, I'm sorry, before you joined the Ilidza Brigade, not the protection regiment. I'm sorry, that's my fault.

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: He submitted a request and perhaps within a month later or so I joined the Ilidza Brigade; i.e., I became a member of the military police of the Ilidza Brigade. So we're talking about a month or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: I'm so glad to be of assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Who was your immediate superior in the military police of the Ilidza Brigade?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: When I first joined, the late Captain Obrad Popadic was the deputy commander. He was my friend and my neighbour in Nedzarici. He was the one who received me, and he asked me to help him with the men and to organise the military police unit in Ilidza since I had completed that training in Han Pijesak. I was a trained military policeman. So I helped him. And the commander of the military police at the time and my superior was Borislav Krajisnik. He was the commander of that unit, of the unit of the military police that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your father, Jovo Sehovac, was the company commander of the 1st Battalion, 3rd Company, of the Ilidza Brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, my father, Jovo Sehovac, was a company commander in the 1st Battalion in Nedzarici, and the 1st Battalion was part of the Ilidza Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it correct that your father was injured on 29 December 1993 when one of his own men threw an explosive device and the shrapnel hit him in the right foot?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: During the war, did you have any relatives who were members of the RS MUP in Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: To try and explain, I'd like to say that when it comes to the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, 360 members of my family, my -- the relatives were members of that corps. They were either with the military or they were members of the military of defence, 360 in total.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. Are you related to Milorad Sehovac, the commander of the 2nd Sarajevo Light Infantry Brigade?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, but we are not close relatives. We are a bit removed in that sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: All right. Are you related to a member of the RS MUP in Ilidza who shares your own name but is older, Goran Sehovac?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: Yes. He was a member of the police at the Kula station. You have to know that the municipality of Serbian Ilidza had a very challenging terrain. It was split into parts during the war. There was a part called Kula-Vojkovic-Krupac and the area in the nearer -- Trnovo --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter missed the second part of that answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was a public police station in Ilidza and another one in Kula. We did not have any physical contact with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes. That Goran Sehovac oversaw the Kula detention facility; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: I don't know. I really don't know. We were not close, hence I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Are you related to Srdjan Sehovac?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, until now it escapes the Chamber what the relevance of family relations in this context is, so if you think it's relevant try to get to the point as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, the reason I'm asking about your relatives is that part of your evidence in a part appears to come from things you've heard, so there may be other evidence in this case or other individuals that may have communicated information that they were aware of. So I'm just asking you to clarify if you know some of these individuals, just so we have it for the record. I appreciate your patience with this. Are you related to Srdjan Sehovac of the RS MUP in Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for helping us with that. I would now like to turn your attention to the monastery in Nedzarici and discuss some instances that took place during your time in the Ilidza Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 1D02008.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: This is a 26 July 1993 disciplinary order from Ilidza Brigade commander Vladimir Radojcic. The person being disciplined is a Novak Popadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Can the Prosecution please have page 2 of the English translation, and same page on the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In the statement of reasons section of this order, there are four events mentioned. I'd like to discuss the first one with you. It's the one that states: "In the immediate vicinity of the monastery in Nedzarici, at about 0830 hours on 26 July 1993, Novak Popadic fired a zolja hand-held rocket launcher at an ambulance, a Toyota vehicle owned by the 1st Battalion, causing considerable ... damage to the vehicle and making it useless." Were you aware of this incident?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: No. Ilidza is big. It was wartime. God knows where I was at that moment. I'm sure that I was not in that territory at the time because I'm not familiar with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it correct that the monastery was located in the zone of responsibility of the 1st Battalion of the Ilidza Brigade?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it correct that members of the brigade held positions in the immediate vicinity of the monastery while they were equipped with zoljas?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: I can only say that the first line was in the barracks just below the monastery. It was held by the 1st Battalion of the Ilidza Brigade of the VRS. The soldiers were equipped, of course, and they had all the weapons necessary to defend themselves from the enemy.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did you ever personally see them equipped with zoljas at the monastery?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: Sir, I am a soldier. The army had everything that was needed to defend from the enemy. If you could only come to Nedzarici, you would be able to see that the distances are never greater than 50 metres including the distance between Nedzarici and the monastery; that is to say, the first line and the monastery.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I -- I was just asking you something really specific: Did you ever see them with zoljas at the monastery? I don't want to dwell on this for long. If you could please listen to my questions.

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: I don't understand the question and I do not understand its importance. You were asking me whether the soldier had a zolja, and it was in the middle of the war. People were being killed in the settlement. Over 300 people were killed in the settlement alone. Of course we were armed. We were the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. Now -- [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did you see the type of equipment that people -- that members of the Ilidza Brigade were armed with at the monastery? I'm asking you if you saw it.

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: I was at the front line. I was a soldier. I was a direct participant. I toured all those front lines towards Stupska Petlja and the city where my father was in command. I was at the front lines. We had automatic weapons of smaller calibre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It seems that your answer is just "yes," you saw it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Are one of those weapons that you saw zoljas, the members of the brigade at the monastery? Did you see that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. Is it correct that Novak Popadic later became a member of the Ilidza assault battalion in 1994 along with yourself?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: Novak Popadic? I don't remember. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution would tender this document into evidence. For the record, the document was also previously used with Witness Radojcic at transcript pages 23267 to -68.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness was asked about this incident. He has no knowledge of it. So I don't believe it's appropriate to enter the document in through cross-examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm doing it a matter for -- well, for expeditiousness. I mean, it was used with a previous witness. I believe it was an associated exhibit to Mr. Radojcic's materials. I would have to confirm that through checking, but at issue is what the witness claimed to have known about the monastery, he's made a statement about it being a medical facility. This document contradicts in part his evidence showing that -- that actually there were armed people at the monastery and engaged -- or at least were equipped with zoljas.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I don't -- Your Honour, where does it say that? It says in the vicinity of the monastery. It does not say any of the stuff that Mr. Weber has just said. That [Overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In the vicinity. In the vicinity of the monastery. In the immediate vicinity of the monastery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, it's not appropriate to introduce this piece of evidence through this witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's look at another example. Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 31027, page 17 of the B/C/S original and page 35 of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Sehovac, coming up before you is a section of the RS military prosecutor's official report on the crime trends in the SRK dated 5 July 1993. I would like to direct your attention to a specific event in this document involving five members of the Ilidza Brigade. I'm going to read it into the record so we have -- we know what it says. "On 6 April 1993 at about 0300 hours in the Nedzarici barracks dormitory, Cvijetic and Domazet arranged to go and pull down the Ilidza municipal government building, and then Domazet went to call for Savic, who was with the battalion commander in his office, telling him: 'Let's go and level the municipal building,' after which they got into a Campagnola jeep and drove up to the monastery in Nedzarici, where Savic woke up Knezevic, a driver, and Zelovic, a T-55 tank crew member, and said that they were going into action. When the crew had taken their position," it's noted in a tank, "they drove it up to the Ilidza municipal government building, where Savic hit the building with a subcalibre shell and about 200 machine-gun bullets, while Cvijetic and Domazet were standing behind the tank firing their pistol and automatic rifle in the direction of the building ..." It then contains information that there were over 2 billion dinars of damage to the Serbian municipality building of Ilidza. Were you aware of this incident as a member of the Ilidza military police?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of this incident, but I do know these people. They were prone to causing problems, and we brought them in on several occasions and they were sanctioned in the military prison. I know who they are but I do not recall the incident. I was not in that territory at the time most likely. Sarajevo covers a large territory. We had several different departments, and I did not deal with this. I wasn't duty-bound to be informed of everything. I know them and I know the -- were under the law several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it correct that a T-55 tank was located at the monastery?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Objection: Misstates the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm entitled to put it to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I don't think as a matter of fact you refer to the statement. You just put a question to the witness. Could you please answer that question. Was a T-55 stationed at the monastery?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not according to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay, well, according to this event in the early hours of the morning, members of the Ilidza Brigade went to the monastery to wake up the tank crew or members of that tank crew which they then found the tank and took it to the Ilidza municipal building. Were you aware of whether the tank crew was stationed at the monastery?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did you see this damage to the Ilidza municipal building?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: Damage was being caused daily by the ABiH shelling, so one couldn't tell what damage was caused by what shell. So in short my answer is no.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'm done with this document. Could the Prosecution please have P775, page 5 of both versions. For the record, this document was marked "not admitted without prejudice" on 28 February 2013. It was an associated exhibit to the statement of Witness Rose, specifically paragraph 183 of P728.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What do you intend to do with the previous document, Mr. Weber?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I -- I wasn't planning on tendering it. I had read --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: -- the incident and I was going to move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That's fine. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Right now I'd like to change topics and talk about humanitarian aid convoys. And I believe the part in the B/C/S that I'm going to be referring to is towards the bottom of the page in front of you on the screen. This is an UNPROFOR weekly situation report for the week of 3 to 10 December 1994. According to this report, it states: "The Serbs continued to blockade Sarajevo for most of the week, then eased off later in the week. Three convoys entered the city on Friday -- the first to arrive in almost a month." The next paragraph then starts: "Serb controls on the road between Sarajevo airport and the city continue to restricts the movement of humanitarian supplies." Now, in your statement, and I'm specifically referring to paragraph 15, you claim that humanitarian aid from the airport passed through your lines and check-points unhindered after a cursory inspection. You've repeated this today in court. I put it to you, based on the document in front of us, that your evidence is inaccurate, and, in fact, there were weeks where humanitarian supplies were not allowed to pass. Do you have any comments?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: Of course I do. Taking into account your position, with all due respect, I believe you are incorrect. Now, what happened? If I may, I'd like to explain. The inhabitants of Ilidza and the members of the Ilidza Brigade never even discussed the issue of preventing the entry of humanitarian aid into Hrasnica and elsewhere. We never even considered it, and we never received any orders to prevent it. Now, what happened when there were no trucks and when there was -- there were no goods entering Sarajevo? If there was an offensive underway or if the ABiH was attacking parts of Nedzarici, as one enters Sarajevo, due to war operations the vehicles were unable to enter the city itself. In all other instances, and I'm telling you the truth, we never even considered prohibiting the entry of anything in order to assist the civilians. That is true and that is the only truth there is that I'm sharing with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: So are you acknowledging that there were weeks where convoys were not allowed to pass?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: It is not true that they were not allowed to enter. It was your assessment -- actually, it was UNPROFOR assessment whether it was safe for the trucks to go through due to wartime operations. If there is a thousand shells in a day landing on Nedzarici, not a civilian can pass through let alone an aid convoy or a truck when there was wartime action between Nedzarici, Ilidza, and Sarajevo airport. I don't know how to explain it in physical terms. It wasn't up to us. We did not prohibit it. It probably only depended on the assessment of the international community whether it was safe or not for the trucks with humanitarian aid to enter Sarajevo or not. It was their assessment, not ours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. You've given some general explanations. I'd like you -- to ask you specifically, do you know why these three convoys were allowed into the city and they were the first to arrive in almost a month? And if you don't know, fine, but you've given some very general answers. I'm putting it to you very specifically, do you know why this happened? Specifically, this incident.

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: I don't understand. What convoy?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. This document indicates that three convoys entered Sarajevo and that they were the first to arrive in almost a month. Do you have any specific knowledge about this event? Those convoys being allowed to enter the city and them being the first ones to arrive in almost a month?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: No, I can't comment on it. I'm not competent enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution will retender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Again, the witness has not shown any personal knowledge for the document. I do not know the reason why it was not admitted the first time around, but with this witness there is nothing that makes this document tied to the testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm offering it to the credibility of the witness. The information is inconsistent with the statements of the witness, and I offer it to assess his credibility. Furthermore, there is additional information that's now been put in this document that wasn't necessarily a part of General Rose's evidence, so therefore we'd be tendering it. It's a document that's now been referred to on multiple occasions during these trial proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is denied. The witness has testified about a matter which is covered to some extent by this document and to that extent there is a link between the testimony and the subject matter covered by the document. Madam Registrar, the number would be? Oh, P --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I would just say the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: -- 65 ter number because it was used with all numbers, so document 08163 keeps or receives number P775.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And P775 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I would now like to discuss the municipality of Vares with you. Is it correct that this municipality is located to the north of Sarajevo, adjacent to the zone of responsibility of the Ilijas Brigade?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, it was the zone of responsibility of the Ilijas Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And just so we don't have any confusion, it's not actually within the zone of responsibility of the Ilidza Brigade but just to the north of it? Or the Ilijas Brigade.

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: Yes. Now, whether it's up north or not, I don't know. But it was in the area of responsibility of the Ilijas Brigade. The Nisici plateau and the surrounding area for the most part was controlled by the Ilijas Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 31024. Your Honours, I just want to -- in order to hopefully head off any confusion once the document comes off. The Prosecution notes there appears to be a possible error in the translation of a date in the first full paragraph of this report as 18 August 1993. The number is not fully clear in the original, but all other references in the document, including the stamp at the bottom, appear to be to June 1993. I will try to seek to clarify some dates with the witness, and I just wanted to alert you to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Sehovac, before you is a SRK command security and intelligence report dated 18 June 1993 from Colonel Marko Lugonja. We can see that the document was sent to multiple SRK brigades, including the Ilidza Brigade. In the first paragraph there is reference to representatives of the HVO from Kiseljak requesting assistance in the form of authorisation to transfer civilians and soldiers from the area of Vares through the territory controlled by the VRS. Do you see this information?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: I apologise, but it is unclear to me. It's a very poor copy and the document is unclear. In my statement I did say that we had received an order from our command, the command of the Ilidza Brigade. The order stated that we should act and save the civilians from Vares, which is probably what you just read out. However, I cannot read it as it is a poor copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. If it helps --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If we could just have the B/C/S version and just the -- the first two paragraphs for right now on the screen before the witness. And I also do have a hard copy for the witness, if it would assist him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And, sir, I'm going to go through the document with you part by part, but are you able to read the information in the first part of the document before you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: It is very unclear, but I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. If any information is not clear to you, please let us know. Can you tell by the information in front of you whether these were the operations you were involved in?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: Could I see the precise date, and maybe you could read out the text and then I'll try to follow?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, the date would be in the heading. It's 18 June 1993. The information I -- I'm at least directing your attention to right now is at -- in the -- it says -- starts with donna 10 [phone], and then the number is unclear, 1993, representatives of the HVO from Kiseljak requested assistance in the form of authorisation to transfer a certain number of civilians and soldiers from the area of Vares through territory controlled by the VRS. I'll go through the numbers then after that, but do you see that information?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. Were these the operations that you were involved with?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, but I didn't see any soldiers. Only civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. Did you learn of any plans for this operation in June of 1993?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: No, simply put: I was a military policeman and it was my duty to implement my command's orders. They ordered that we should save these people and we went to save them, to save the Croat civilians, or rather civilians of Croat ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. The next sentence says: [As read] "Representatives of the HVO and the civilian authorities in Kiseljak requested the transfer of approximately 3.000 civilians and approximately 400 soldiers in 20 buses from Vares." Were you aware of this request?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: I do know that all of the civilians were transported to Kiseljak on board buses, and I also know that our civilian authorities offered all of them to remain in RS territory. And I'm happy to be able to explain that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, sir --

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: And they were also offered --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: -- to send their children to schools --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, if you could please focus precisely on my questions. I'm asking you were you aware of the request by the HVO representatives? If you don't, it's fine; if you did, please let us know.

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: I did not deal with requests specifically. I worked in the field. We transferred the civilians to Kiseljak, and we provided security for them en route to their free territory as they had requested. It was probably pursuant to their request. Our order was to secure them, take them out of Vares, and escort them to the free territory held by Croat forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. I want to talk a little bit about the order that you received. According to this document in front of you, the Croats' request was forwarded to the Main Staff of the VRS, which decided as follows: That the requested number of civilians and soldiers may be transferred in the following manner, and then there is three items; that the civilians should be transported separately and in the first rounds of buses; second, the transport of HVO soldiers is to be allowed only after the civilians have been transported. The soldiers are to be transported unarmed and without any especially conspicuous insignia of belonging to the army; the third item, the soldiers' weapons and ammunition are to be transported in a special convoy separate from the soldiers. Did you receive this order?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: No. I was in charge of saving the civilians. We completed the task successfully and then we returned to the base. I suppose that somebody else did the rest. We were in charge of one part of the job, we did it successfully, we saved the civilians, and our -- I am proud as a soldier of the VRS for having saved many mothers, many children in that territory. I take pride in my words, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. In your statement you say you received an order from the superior command to undertake the transfer of the civilians. When you refer to "superior commander," are you then referring to just your immediate command in the Ilidza Brigade?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: I'm talking about the Ilidza Brigade, yes. I was a soldier of the Ilidza Brigade, but there was also a hierarchy. I suppose that the Ilidza Brigade received its order to carry out a task which they conveyed to the soldiers, and we acted upon the order of our command. It was not transferred. It was assistance. We assisted those people, me personally and all of my soldiers. We all acted humanely.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm sorry to cut you off but you actually answered my question right out of the gate there. I do want to move so that we get you home hopefully after today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one additional question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The order that you are talking about, that is to assist the civilians, was that a written order or was that an oral order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We had radio sets. We did not receive written orders. We had radio sets, all of us did, in all of the bases, and we received a coded order as to what to do and how to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the simple answer is then it was an oral order communicated through a radio. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: When did you carry out this order that you received? When was it that you moved the civilians from Vares?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: Late in the day. One part of that, the part that we were in charge of, we received that late in the day. We received one part sometime late in the afternoon and the other part during the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Do you remember what month this was in 1993?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: No, I can't remember. I can't remember. It was a long time ago. A long time ago, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. Toward the end of this document, there are references to the Ilidza SJB. Is it correct that members of the public security service of the RS MUP also participated in these operations?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: Of course, of course. Ilidza was a very compact unit. The troops co-operated with the civilian police. We carried out tasks together, especially when it came to the defence of the territory and saving the civilians. I have to tell you that the civilian and military authorities co-operated in saving those people, which means that the police was also involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In paragraph 13 of your statement, you state: "The police from the corps as well as senior officers were present on this occasion." Are you referring to this occasion where you carried out the orders from Vares? It's unclear from the statement what occasion you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: That area in Brgule was very narrow as you go from Vares via Brgule. There was a lot of troops deployed there. The corps military police were also there. They had come to assist with the task ordered by the command of the Ilidza Brigade, and they in turn had received that order from the main command; i.e., the general himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it correct that --

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: Because it was not only a task of the Ilidza Brigade. All the brigades had to take part in the action to save the civilians from there. It was a major operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it correct that the occasion that you are referring to is the occasion where Croats were transferred from Vares?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: This is not what I think. I was there and we helped the Croatian population to get out of there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, just help me out here. If you look at paragraph 13, what occasion are you referring to? Are you referring to Vares?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: If you refer to paragraph --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: If you refer to paragraph 13 of his statement --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- you should call up it on the screen because he is looking at the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes. I am referring to your statement which I see you have in front of you.

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, paragraph -- yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And in that paragraph of your statement you're referring to the occasion that you've been talking about with respect to Vares?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The answer of the witness does not appear on the transcript. Do I understand that you confirmed that the occasion you refer to in paragraph 13 was the occasion where citizens of Vares were assisted in leaving?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. I tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 31024 receives number P6692, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Mr. Weber, when you quoted the first line where you said there may be some mistake about the month, you refer to it as the 10th of what you think, but even the number 10 --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- may be something like 18 --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Eighteen -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- or so. Therefore, if there is any dispute about that, I just want to put on the record that the Chamber does not immediately, or at least I do not immediately, agree with you that it's for certain a 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I actually agree with you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I think I said it wrong and thank you for catching it. It's the Prosecution's position that the correct date would be 18 June 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Witness, one additional question in relation to this document. Was this what you say major operation the only time you assisted in the escort of Croats from Vares? That this was a one-time operation? A similar thing did not happen in the same year at other moments? You understand my question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Or is there a translation issue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When it comes to Vares -- I understood your question. When it comes to Vares, it was a major operation. A very demanding operation, Your Honour. And it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I just was interested to know whether such an operation - that is, a large number of civilians moving out of Vares, where you were involved in it - whether that was the only time that you were involved in such an operation in relation to Vares?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we are talking a major operation, then yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, I'm looking at the clock. It's time for a break. Where are we as far as time is concerned?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I will definitely finish today in the next session. I think if there is only 20 minutes, I will probably use most of the next session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I will ask Madam Registrar how much time you have used until now. But we'll hear that during the break. Witness, we'll take a break of 20 minutes. You'll be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And we resume at 20 minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I correct a transcript reference from earlier today?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, at page 48, line 18, I believe today's transcript records me as referring to P55. The correct reference would be P355.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's then hereby corrected. Mr. Weber, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have P2006, page 3 of the B/C/S original and page 2 of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I just want to broaden out from Vares a little bit and ask you more generally about some information. Before you is Directive 5 from General Mladic, dated 25 June 1993. Specifically, I'd like you -- to focus your attention on section 3 that discusses the battle that is raging between the Muslims and Croats. Just stopping here, in June of 1993 were you aware that the Muslims and Croats were fighting one another?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: No, we had other problems. That was not one of them, and I really did not understand because the Muslims and the Croats tied their flags together in Sarajevo. That had never been the case before. I didn't realise why that was happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go on, and I want to focus you on a particular part of section 3. It's where General Mladic states: "The VRS is trying to exploit this conflict and do everything to prevent that the weapons used by the HVO" from "falling into Muslim hands, but rather by reasoned military and political moves to force the Croats to turn these weapons and their positions over to us." Do I understand correctly that you were not aware of this objective while you were carrying out operations in Vares?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: You have to know that Ilidza, being Ilidza where I was, co-operated with the Croatian forces throughout the war; the forces in Kiseljak, that is. We literally never waged war in that part, so I don't understand your question. In that part we were on good terms. We did not attack each other at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: My question was very simple and it was just: Were you or were you not aware of what General Mladic says in section 3 of this directive?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: No, I do not understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have P358, page 243 of the B/C/S original and page 240 of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Didn't you understand the question or -- the question was rather clear, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I'm listening. I'm listening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, what Mr. Weber puts to you is that General Mladic in this notebook states that: "The VRS is trying to exploit this conflict and do everything to prevent that the weapons used by the HVO not fall into Muslim hands but rather by recent military and political moves to force the Croats to turn these weapons and their positions over to us." Now, the question is: Were you or were you not aware of this position as written down by Mr. Mladic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Before you is an 8 July 1993 entry from one of General Mladic's notebooks concerning a meeting with President Slobodan Milosevic. According to these notes, Radovan Karadzic, General Panic, Prime Minister Sainovic, and Ivica Stanisic are also present at this meeting. According to the notes, General Mladic records President Karadzic as stating: "Help the Croats in order to force the Muslims to agree on a division of Bosnia." Were you aware that the Bosnian Serb leadership wanted to help the Croats in 1993 in order to force the Muslims to divide Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 31025.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Coming up before you is a 20 August 1993 letter from the president of the Vares municipality to President Franjo Tudjman and others. According to the first paragraph of the letter, the letter communicates the concerns of thousands of Croats from Vares who are worried about unacceptable solutions being imposed on them and new attempts to separate the Croatian population in this area from the rest of the Croatian people. I just wanted you to see that for context. I'd like to now go down and direct your attention to the fourth paragraph, where the letter states: "The Croats of Vares are firm in their decision to continue to lead their own life on their own land. That is why they tried and succeeded in preserving Vares for themselves, and not for those who attack it." In your evidence you have claimed that the civilians in Vares wanted to leave. I put it to you that this is not accurate based on what we see in this letter; is this correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: We obviously did not understand each other. Yes, in this letter we can see that the Croats wanted to remain in Vares, but they were driven out by the ABiH not the VRS. The VRS saved them. They were driven from Vares and attacked. The town and the villages around it were attacked by the ABiH, expelling Croats. The Croats had to leave. God forbid they had stayed. There would have been many victims. We saved them and I'm proud of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: So you acknowledge that the Croats -- the local Croat, Bosnian Croat population of Vares did not want to leave?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: They lived there. They spent their lives in Vares and they were driven out by the army of BiH. We were simply observers who came to their rescue. We saved them. We saved the children. You have to acknowledge that. You have to acknowledge that, sir, that we saved the children. As a boy who was a soldier at the time, I'm proud of it, and you have to be aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: We'll --

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: I'd rather not discuss it any longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. We're actually going to go through some more information about that. I understand correctly that your evidence is that the local Croat population of Vares did not want to leave.

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: Not until they were attacked. That is the short answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: A little later in the sixth paragraph of this letter, it states that all other solutions, impossible political bargains, would be --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No speaking aloud, no speaking aloud.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm told the B/C/S translation has ceased. The French channel is blending into the B/C/S channel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, could we continue. Let's take it that -- yes, translation is okay now again. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'll start again.

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: [In English] okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: A little later in the sixth paragraph of the letter, it states that all other solution, impossible political bargains, would be interpreted by the Croatian people as a betrayal of their interests. Were you aware of whether the local Croat population of Vares felt betrayed by their own leaders because of an agreement with the VRS?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that time we did not consider that. We simply followed our orders and tasks. The only thing that was on our minds was to save their lives, to save those people who were incapable of defending themselves from the aggression on Vares launched by the ABiH. That's what I know and that's the only thing I can say and confirm. Any other thing referring to politics, what was agreed with Tudjman, what was agreed to by the HVO, I don't know. It was high politics for me at the time. I was simply a direct participant who assisted those people to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution would tender 65 ter 31025 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, this witness has not identified knowledge of any of the document's terms. It's not sent to him. We think it's not a proper document to come in through the cross-examination of this witness and the fashion that it's been used, to draw half-conclusions from text that doesn't say what the Prosecution says it says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Defence has now led evidence about Vares, a municipality not in the indictment. And I'm attempting to lead some information to give the Chamber a proper context so it may adjudicate events that relate to this matter. The witness has partially acknowledged certain sentiments the local Croat population and his lack of awareness of certain things at higher levels. I believe this document is relevant. It does have nexus to the topic in evidence of this witness and it is important for the Chamber to have this material in order for the Chamber to properly adjudicate events that happened in this municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, I didn't hear Mr. Ivetic complaining about it not being an indictment municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's -- for other reasons I think he objected to admission.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And the reason I mention it is because there is not much other information so far in the record about this. So to say or possibly later submit that there is a certain purpose of operations in Vares based on minimal evidence led by a Defence witness and then not enable the Prosecution to tender appropriately information that relates to those events, I think would be quite limiting and would leave an incomplete record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The objection is denied. The document covers events which are closely related to events the witness testified about and that's the reason why the Chamber denies the objection. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 31025 receives number P6693, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P6693 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And then, sir, I'd like to ask you just in general a more specific time-period. Do you recall whether or not when you engaged in this operation to move civilians from Vares, whether that was in the summer -- I'm sorry, can you hear me? Was that operation in the summer or the fall of 1993? Was it warm out or was it getting cold?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: I said a moment ago that I do not recall the exact date, but it was neither warm nor cold, similar to the weather conditions here today. Perhaps that's how I can explain. It was rather grey.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'll just precisely put it -- a time-period to you. Do you recall where you were at late October 1993 and early November 1993?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: Believe me when I say that it was a long time ago, but it was within that range of two to three months.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: When you say --

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: I don't know the date. I cannot say anything regard that. It's been 20 years and many things happened in the meantime. Whatever I said would be untrue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'm not asking for a specific date, but just said: "But it was within the range of the two to three months." What is the "it" that you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: It concerns the event you're asking me about.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: It was within that range, that's when it happened. I don't know the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And what months, two to three months, are you referring to? To the best of your recollection.

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: September, October, around that time. Those two to three months. In that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. One last document, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 31022.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: This is a letter from the archbishop of Vrhbosna to President Franjo Tudjman dated 31 October 1993. In the third paragraph of the letter the archbishop discusses an alleged statement from a commander in a municipality in Central Bosnia who stated: "We have an agreement made with the Serbian side. They will offer the HVO its assistance, cleanse the area controlled by us, and the Serbs will make it possible for us to move the Croats from Kiseljak, Kresevo, Vares, Vitez, and Busovaca. We shall hand those areas over to the Chetniks. Our bosses and the Serbian bosses have agreed on solving these areas in this way."

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And if the Prosecution could have the next page in the English translation only.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In the middle of the next paragraph, the archbishop states in reference to the HVO: "They constantly claim that they keep receiving such orders. I am no longer confident that the Croatian politics protects us. We feel that we have been sacrificed and condemned to a slow death at that." I'm showing you this material for context. But based on this document and the other materials we have seen today, I put it to you that the local Croat population of Vares did not want to move but did so not because of attacks by the ABiH but because of an agreement between the Croatian and Bosnian Serb leadership which further served the Bosnian Serb interests of dividing Bosnia. Do you have any comments or any other comments other than the ones you've made today?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: No problem. You are obviously good at what you do, and you're trying to put a twist on the issue of transferring people. Out of respect, I'd like to explain. The Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina attacked the territory. It is the only fact, the only truth in all of this. That was the only thing I was interested in. Now, what Puljic wrote, what other high politicians wrote is their own problem. I was a soldier. I saw an armed force killing people and torching villages, and I had to help the people. I did. It was true that the ABiH wanted to approach the Serb lines to a minimum distance because shortly afterwards they did approach our lines and killed several of our soldiers at Brgule where the area through which we pulled out the Croats. So I'm only speaking from the military point of view. I do not wish to discuss any high politics and the statements of senior politicians. I would rather not go into it. I have nothing to do with it, and I don't even know what the context is that you're putting me in. Why should I discuss what Vinko Puljic discussed with other politicians. I do not wish to comment and I'm not competent to address it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: At this time the Prosecution tenders the exhibit into evidence for the same reasons as the last document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The witness knows nothing about the document itself, but I would add, if -- given that we've learned the Prosecution's position on this, I would inquire of the Prosecution when they will be dropping the genocide counts in the indictment, if it's -- if population exchanges were due to an agreement, when will the genocide count be dropped?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: -- if you'll forgive me, I'm not going to respond to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber responds to the first line, Mr. Ivetic, you spoke, that the witness knows nothing about the document itself. And on the basis of that, that objection is denied as a reason for nonadmission for the same reasons as related to the previous ones; that is, that it's related to the reasons the witness has given for the operations. Madam Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 31022 receives number P6694, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P6694 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And, sir, I just have one more question left for you today. And it relates to the assault battalion that you joined in early 1994. Is it correct that until 17 April 1994, the commander of the assault battalion was Slobodan Janjic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: Yes. The assault battalion of the Ilidza Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. And is it correct that Mr. Janjic was killed during operations near Gorazde on the 17th of April, 1994?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: Slobodan Janjic, aka Baubau [phoen], was the commander of the assault battalion. He was killed in the theater defending the territory of Republika Srpska. It was near Gorazde. In that area. I did not take part in that operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: That's all I have for the witness, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Just one question, Your Honours, in redirect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, at temporary transcript page 69, lines 3 to 7, you said that an order came from the main commander for the Croat civilians to be assisted from the general himself, what general were you referring to? That's not in your statement. That was in the transcript. You were testifying and you said that the order came from the general himself and I was asking to which general you meant?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, could you assist us? Because page 3, I think, is still the submissions made by Mr. Lukic this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I thought I said page 69 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. Yes, that's...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- lines 3 to 7. Perhaps it would assist if I read the full answer for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, this is the answer that is recorded in the transcript: "The area in Brgule was very narrow as you go from Vares via Brgule. There was a lot of troops deployed there. The corps military police was also there. They had come to assist with the task ordered by the command of the Ilidza Brigade, and they in turn had received that order from the main command, i.e., the general himself." And my question was simply, sir, when you say "i.e., the general himself," who were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SEHOVAC
utterances.text: May I? I had General Ratko Mladic in mind in agreement with the civilians authorities in order to save the lives of civilians. That is my short answer. It was received by the command of the Ilidza Brigade. Not me, personally. I was just a soldier. The command conveyed the order to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have answered the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, that's all I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you again, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Witness, I've got one question for you: Were there only Croats living in Vares or were there other ethnic groups living in Vares as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see, I didn't live there. I hail from Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Vares was foreign territory to me. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You don't know. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have no further questions. I take it that this one question from the Bench will not have triggered any --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Not for the Defence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Witness, this concludes your testimony in this Court. I would like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague and for having answered all the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench and I wish you a safe return home again. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I am glad to have been of assistance in finding the truth, if successful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to use the remaining two minutes to deal with witness scheduling. On the 30th of July of this year through an informal communication, the Chamber received a schedule from the Defence informing it of the witnesses who would be testifying in the last week of August and the first week of September. Last Thursday evening, the Chamber received an updated Defence witness schedule which contains changes to the 30th of July schedule. It did not receive this schedule from the Defence but it received it through Madam Registrar. It was only through her diligence that the Chamber was informed of the latest changes to the schedule. On the 8th of July exactly the same scenario occurred. As a result, the Chamber specifically instructed the Defence to send any changes to the witness schedule as soon as possible in writing to Chamber's staff. I would like to refer you to transcript pages 23643 to 23644 and 23664 to 23665. The Chamber takes this opportunity to remind the Defence, once again, of its instruction to inform the Chamber in writing of any changes to the witness schedule as soon as practically possible. And I must stress the importance of this information to the Chamber's work in preparing these hearings and urge the Defence to strictly adhere to this instruction in the future. We adjourn for the day and we will resume tomorrow, Tuesday, the 26th of August, 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 26th day of August, 2014, at 9.30 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.16 p.m.,
